en.title: Demonstrative pronouns
en.summary: A demonstrative pronoun points without naming.

paragraphs: A demonstrative pronoun points to a person or thing and replaces the noun. English has four forms: this and these for things that are near, and that and those for things that are far.
Demonstratives show distance in space or time and have singular and plural forms. The same words are used as determiners before a noun: this book, those people. As pronouns, they stand alone.
This and these can also refer to the present moment or to what you are about to say: Listen to this. That and those refer to what has already been said or is over: That was a good idea.

blocks.html:
Pronoun (alone)Determiner (before a noun)
This is easy.This exercise is easy.
Those are mine.Those shoes are mine.
I like that.I like that song.

items: On the telephone: **Hello, this is Anna.** (not: I am Anna)
To introduce a person: **This is my friend Tom.**
To avoid repeating a noun: **The weather in Spain is warmer than that in England.**
In comparisons: **Prices here are higher than those in the north.**
Wrong: **These is my book.** Right: **This is my book.**
Wrong: **I like this ones.** Right: **I like these ones.** (or: these)
Wrong: **What is this? Those are mine.** Make the number agree: **These are mine.**
